2027-02-14.title: First Sunday of Lent
readings: God's covenant with Noah, set free from the waters of the flood
Your ways, O Lord, are love and truth to those who keep your covenant
Baptism, which this prefigured, now saves you

2027-02-14.alt: Year B. The Rite of Election of catechumens for Easter Baptism is celebrated today in many dioceses. The memorial of Sts Cyril and Methodius is not kept this year because it falls on Sunday. No Gloria. Liturgical colour: violet.
2027-02-14.verse: And the Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. He was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts; and the angels waited on him.
theo: Every First Sunday of Lent takes us into the desert with Jesus, but each year tells it differently. Mark, in Year B, is the briefest of all: two verses. “And the Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. He was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts; and the angels waited on him.” No dialogue, no list of temptations. Just the scene: the Son, newly anointed at the Jordan, sent by the Spirit into the place of testing. He is the new Israel, who spent forty years in the wilderness and failed; he is the new Adam, who was tempted in a garden and fell. Jesus is tempted in a wilderness and stands firm. And the wild beasts around him and the angels serving him recall paradise restored: the harmony of creation that Isaiah foresaw, when “the wolf shall live with the lamb.”

The first reading opens with another new beginning. After the flood, God makes a covenant not only with Noah and his family but “with every living creature”: “never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood.” As its sign he sets his bow in the clouds: “When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant.” The bow, once a weapon of war, now hangs unstrung in the sky, pointed away from the earth. It is a sign of God's peace. St Peter sees in the flood a figure of baptism: in the ark “eight persons, were saved through water. And baptism, which this prefigured, now saves you.” Christ, “put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit”, has suffered “for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, in order to bring you to God.”

After the desert Jesus comes into Galilee proclaiming: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news.” This is Lent in one sentence. Today in cathedrals the catechumens who will be baptized at Easter are chosen and enrolled: the Rite of Election. For them Lent is the final preparation for the waters; for the rest of us, it is a return to the waters we have already passed through. The Psalm gives our prayer: “Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths.” We do not go into this desert alone. The Spirit leads us, the angels serve us, and the One who was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, goes before us.
conn: Noah's rain fell forty days (Genesis 7:12); Moses fasted forty days on Sinai (Exodus 34:28); Elijah walked forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8); Israel wandered forty years (Deuteronomy 8:2).
Mark's strong verb (ekballō) is the same used for casting out demons: the Spirit thrusts Jesus into the battle with Satan.
Only Mark mentions them; they recall Adam among the animals and Isaiah's vision of peace (Isaiah 11:6–9).
The Hebrew word for rainbow is the same as for a war bow; God hangs up his weapon as a sign of peace.
The early Church saw the eighth day, the day of resurrection, in the eight saved in the ark; many ancient baptisteries are eight-sided.
On this Sunday the bishop chooses the catechumens for Easter sacraments; their names are written in the Book of the Elect.
altar: The Lord who was fed by angels in the desert now feeds us with the Bread of Angels for our forty days.
Baptism brought us through the waters; the Eucharist sustains us on the journey to Easter, when we will renew our baptismal promises.

fathers: In Christ you were tempted, and in him you overcame. He took to himself our temptation so as to give us his victory; if in him we are tempted, in him we conquer the devil.
The flood was a figure of baptism: sin was drowned, the just were saved, and the dove brought the olive branch of peace, as the Spirit descends on the baptized.
It was not unworthy of our Redeemer to be tempted, for he came to be killed; he overcame our temptations by his own, as he overcame our death by his death.
magis: The temptations of Jesus: the new Adam who remained faithful; Lent unites us to his forty days.
The covenant with Noah: God's covenant with all the nations.
The ark of Noah as a prefiguring of salvation by Baptism.

2027-02-14.prayer: Grant, almighty God, through the yearly observances of holy Lent, that we may grow in understanding of the riches hidden in Christ and by worthy conduct pursue their effects. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you went into the desert, were tempted and overcame. Lead us by your Spirit through these forty days; keep us faithful to our baptism; strengthen the elect who will be baptized at Easter; and bring us all to the joy of your resurrection. Amen.

family.explain: The Holy Spirit led Jesus into the desert for forty days. Satan tempted him, but Jesus said no to Satan. Wild animals were near, and angels took care of him. Then Jesus said: turn back to God and believe the good news!

illus: A young mother in Thiruvalla was preparing for Baptism at Easter. On the First Sunday of Lent she stood before the bishop as her name was called and written in the Book of the Elect. She said afterwards: for months I felt alone in my desert of questions. Today I heard my name, and I knew the whole Church was walking with me to the water.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, every First Sunday of Lent takes us into the desert with Jesus. This year Mark tells it in just two verses: the Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. He was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts; and the angels waited on him (Mark 1:12–13).

Israel was tested forty years in the wilderness and failed. Adam was tested in a garden and fell. Jesus, the new Adam and the true Israel, is tested and stands firm. And around him are wild beasts at peace and angels serving: a glimpse of paradise restored.

In the first reading God makes a covenant with Noah and with every living creature, and sets his bow in the clouds as a sign (Genesis 9:13). The bow, a weapon of war, now hangs in the sky as a sign of peace.

St Peter tells us that the ark, in which eight persons were saved through water, prefigured baptism, which now saves you (1 Peter 3:20–21). Christ suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Today the elect, who will be baptized at Easter, are called by name.

Then Jesus proclaims: the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news (Mark 1:15). That is Lent in one sentence: turn around, and trust the good news.

We do not enter this desert alone. The Spirit leads us, the angels serve us, and Jesus, who was tempted as we are, goes ahead of us. Let us pray with the Psalm: make me to know your ways, O LORD. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus stayed in the desert for forty days. Satan tried to make him do wrong, but Jesus said no! Angels came to help him.
When you are tempted to do something wrong, say: Jesus, help me! He will help you say no.
